replying_to: Replying to Differential Privacy with Manifold Data Dependency
display_title: Official Review of Paper2731 by Reviewer R4Hw

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tries to adapt differential privacy concepts to data correlated through a manifold dependency. However, their concept of privacy relates more to statistical inference than an actual privacy guarantee and fundamentally misunderstand the distinction between personal and private information.
content.main_review:
This paper, like a number of papers on the 'problems' with correlations and differential privacy is flawed. The paper does not do a good job of clarifying exactly what the problem is, and in what sense differential privacy, or the specific neighbourhood definition used, creates it.

I recall one interpretation of differential privacy:
"Regardless of external knowledge, an adversary with access to the sanitized database draws the same conclusions whether or not my data is included in the original database"
So, to take the extreme example where everybody's data is exactly the same. Then of course, knowing the data of one person in the database reveals everybody's data. More generally, if there are strong correlations, then knowing everybody else's data gives some information about you. This is not related to differential privacy. Even if your own data is encrypted or not even included in the actual database, somebody can still learn a lot about you. So what is the problem?

McSherry has a nice blog post where he talks about this. The one-line takeaway is "However, differential privacy's guarantees only mask the presence of those records received from each user, they do not mask larger statistical trends that may reveal information about each user. "

https://github.com/frankmcsherry/blog/blob/master/posts/2016-08-29.md

I think it is not reasonable to say that manifold (or other correlations) are a problem for differential privacy. You should instead change the definition of what you want to keep private. It is perhaps interesting to consider a neighbourhood definition in a manifold, which is what this paper is doing (as the authors helpfully clarified), but since the standard definition of neighbourhood where x N x' if x has one more/less datapoint than x' also suffices for this setting. (The definition where x differ only in one point may not be applicable at all in a manifold setting, as no such neighbouring points may exist).

If you want to go in that direction, then there is a nice set of papers  which define a different notion of privacy, precisely for the case where you need strong statistical inference guarantees. See e.g. 
- Composition properties of inferential privacy for time-series data
- Pufferfish: A framework for mathematical privacy definitions
 -Pufferfish privacy mechanisms for correlated data

In summary, the main example is not sufficiently rigorous, and the paper's main claims are misleading. The authors do not explain why the standard more/less records definition does not apply here, and what a new definition offers. If the paper is rewritten appropriately, it might be a worthwhile contribution. You must:

(a) specify what you are trying to protect
(b) show why one of the two standard neighbourhood definitions doesn't protect it
(c) show that your definition does.

Thanks for the discussion
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper is misleading and insufficiently motivated.

content.title: Rebuttal: the suggested approach is in line with our treatment; the suggested reference actually confirms our finding.
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time in evaluating our work, and for the in-depth comments. We appreciate the constructive comments on related differential privacy frameworks with correlated data. However, we believe unfortunately there seem to be significant misunderstandings of our work in the review.  In fact, the key argument and evidence in asserting our paper to be wrong, are actually in line with what we already accomplished in the paper,  for reasons outlined below. 

 

First of all, our work is not about probabilistically correlated data entries in differential privacy, but on deterministic manifold dependency in the dataset.
 
(1) Example 1 clearly shows that deterministic manifold dependency leads to a change of differential privacy budget by explicit and direct computation. 

(2) Definition 4 and Definition 5 (p3) set the precise problem definition of our work, where the manifold adjacency and the resulting notion of differential privacy are carefully defined. 

(3) Section 4 shows that  in cloud-based control systems, the manifold dependency arises inherently from the system dynamics, and our approach offers a provably feasible solution (Theorem 3, p8). 

In fact, the comment says ``It would be interesting instead perhaps to consider a neighbourhood definition in a manifold, but this is not what this paper is doing.`` Looking into Definition 4 of our manuscript, a neighbourhood definition in a manifold is exactly what we are trying to accomplish. Please note that Definition 4 is literally  termed Manifold $\mu$-Adjacency with the new neighborhood is denoted as ${\rm Adj}(\mu, \mathcal{C}_d)$. Therefore, we believe the assertion  that ``the paper is wrong`` unfortunately might be based on fundamental misunderstandings of our work. 

 
Second, this manifold dependency is not related to encrypted data or data not included in the actual database.  In fact, the manifold dependency is a special affine manifold data structure in the database. As shown in Eqs (15) -- (17),  Section 4, such affine manifold structure is specified for cloud-base control systems, and any adversary with knowledge of the system dynamics will possess such knowledge. Then, the challenge lies in this manifold structure significantly affects the achievable differential privacy levels as shown in Example 1. In the cited blog by McSherry, the value of studying differential privacy with correlated data is also acknowledged, where a full takeaway says the following:

(McSherry Blog) ``However, differential privacy's guarantees only mask the presence of those records received from each user, they do not mask larger statistical trends that may reveal information about each user. This distinction can lead to degradation in expected privacy levels especially when applied to real-world datasets that manifest natural dependence owing to various social, behavioral, and genetic relationships between users.``

This second sentence from this blog, echos and confirms our observation and problem setup. 

In summary,  deterministic manifold dependency is a non-trivial and useful extension of differential privacy for both theories and real-world applications. The contributions of our work lie in a novel and complete treatment to the privacy analysis and mechanism design for such systems. Our efforts are actually in line with the reviewer's suggestion of ``a neighborhood definition in a manifold" for an interesting study, and the key insight outlined in the suggested McSherry Blog.  

In addition,  we thank the reviewer for pointing out the relevant references on Pufferfish privacy mechanisms, which are certainly very helpful.  In the revised manuscript, we have cited this framework and added discussions on their connections with our work.

content.title: Understood the response, but the paper is misleading
content.comment:
"We present an example to show that when entries in the input data are independent or dependent in
an affine manifold, the achievable differential privacy levels may be quite different."

But in fact the differential privacy guarantee in this example holds perfectly well. What you are measuring is not differential privacy.

It does not matter if $x_1$, $x_2$ are independent or not. The only thing that DP says is that, if the output of the mechanism is y, then, for all $x,x'$:

\[
P_M(y | x) \leq P_M(y | x') e^\epsilon.
\]

In your example, even if $x_1 = x_2$, this makes no difference. What McSherry is saying, which you are still ignoring, is that DP is a definition about an individual's contribution to the database. If the individual's data can already be deduced from everybody else's database entries, that does NOT mean that differential privacy is compromised.

So, the example you have does not prove this rigorously. The mechanism that you specify is in fact a local differentially private mechanism, since you release the original data with some noise added. If the output values are $y_1, y_2$, then we assume that the local-DP property holds, we have:

\[
P_M(y_i | x_i) \leq P_M(y_i | x'_i) e^\epsilon
\]
Now let us consider composition, where the data differs in one co-ordinate. 
\[
P_M(y | x) = \prod_i  P_M(y_i | x) = \prod_i  P_M(y_i | x_i)
\]
by the fact that the mechanism is local. Consqeuently the differential privacy property also holds, no matter what the dependencies between $x_i$ are. So, if we consider any $x,x'$ that are neighbouring in the standard neighbourhood definition, it works.

In your setting, in fact, $x_1$ determines $x_2$ and vice-versa.  So, the concept of neighbourhood must be carefully defined. There are two standard concepts, one of which implies the other. The stronger one is $x, x'$ are neighbours if one entry in $x$ is not in $x'$. Let's call this N1. The weaker one is that $x,x'$ differ in one entry. Let's call this N2. In fact, if $x,x'$ are N2 neighbours, then they are also 2-N1 neighbours.

I must strongly emphasize that the concept of DP still works fine in your example. In your setting, $N1 neighbourhood works. If $x_1$'s data has been released, then it makes no dfifference if $x_2$'s data is released. If $x_1$'s data has not been relased, then again $x_2$'s release is DP. So when exaxctly is this concept useful?

You should rewrite your example, similarly to what I wrote, so that it actually disscusses the fundamental problem, which is that standard neighbourhood definitions do not apply in this setting.

You should in particular clarify what the concept of privacy you wish to maintain is, and how it differs or generalises DP with the standard neighbourhood concept. Why is the new neighbourhood concept needed? When can it be used? H

In addiiton, you should read the 'correlated DP' work very carefully to separate the papers that are correct from those that are not. I think it's safest to go with the Pufferfish/Blowfish line of work. A lot of the 'correlated DP' stuff is incorrect.

So I think the paper should not be accepted until after all these recommended changes have been made. You can submit it to another venue. I recommend submitting it to a privacy-focused venue or workshop first.

content.title: Further responses
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer again very much for the further comments. We also thank the reviewer's suggestion in submitting this work to a new venue. 

Now we (kind of) understand that the comments did not try to dismiss all our contributions as it appeared to be in the first place. In the end, we specified a new adjancency for queries over affine manifolds, and developed systemic results for it.

We also would like to clarify a few things.

First of all, our work focuses on linear mechanism $M(x)=Fx + \gamma$. For convenience, in the motivating Example 1 we let $F=I$. In this special case, the two outputs of the mechanism can be regarded as releasing $x_1$ and $x_2$, respectively, which leads the reviewer to misunderstand that our work studies a local differentially private mechanism. In fact, throughout the paper we don't impose any restrictions on the matrix $F$, for example $F=[1,1;0,1]$. In other words, this work does not study a local differentially private mechanism.

Secondly, we believe that the reviewer misunderstood our definition of data adjacency/neighborhood. To be precise, our adjacency is defined on the distance metric, which does not belong to the mentioned N1 nor N2. 

In particular, we did not claim in any way in our framework that differential privacy will "not work" on affine manifolds. What we were suggesting is that if we follow the regular differential privacy adjacency, the resulting privacy level will not hold. This is in line with the Blowfish framework on "policy" and McSherry's comment.

Your comment is more on the terminology choice on correlation or dependency. However, this manifold is just "constraints that may be known about the data" [Blowfish]

content.title: Ironing out the differences
content.comment:
Thanks again.

Mathematically there is nothing wrong, but the way you presented your claims in the paper was misleading

I do not disagree about your neighbourhood. It is neither N1 nor N2. I am asking merely 'if you used N1, could you avoid this problem? Even if xi are constrained to be eg. on the surface of a sphere, N1 is still a useful neighbourhood. You can add/remove points from the surface to your dataset without violating the constraints. What would the result be?'

As for the metric, there are a few papers that specifically look at differential privacy in metric spaces e.g. 'Differential Privacy for Metric Spaces', with appropriate neighbourhood definitions. Some of them focus on specific domains, like geographical information, and others on general statistical settings where the input domain can be unbounded (and hence boundedness is replaced by a metric)

Again, the problem is one mainly of semantics and interpretation. I think if you frame your paper more properly with relation to Pufferfish and the metric space work, it is an interesting question to look at efficiently answering queries over manifolds under differential privacy. I can update my score, but I still think that the paper should best be resubmitted and at least the introduction thoroughly rewritten.

content.title: Thanks for the prompt feedback
content.comment:
Thanks for the prompt feedback. Now everything is clear, and we understand our work has been essentially an extension of the Blowfish He et al. (2014), and work on differential privacy over metric spaces Holohan et al. (2015) .  We have thoroughly rewritten the introduction and the terminology throughout the paper. Please see the rebuttal revision. 

We also would like to clarify there is subtle but important differences between our work and differential privacy over metric spaces. 

For example, Holohan et al. (2015)  has considered databases with entries defined over a metric space $(\mathcal{U}, \rho)$, where $\rho$ is a metric Holohan et al. (2015). In this way, an $n$-dimensional  database takes values from $\mathcal{D}^n$ with $\mathcal{D}\in \mathcal{U}$ Holohan et al. (2015). Note that the affine manifold $\mathcal{C}_d \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ in the current study can not be written in the form of a Cartesian product $\mathcal{D}^n$.  With $\mathcal{C}_d$, now there is inherent geometry between the entries in a database, while a database in $\mathcal{D}^n$ has homogeneous geometry on individual entries. 

Moreover, for any two databases $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^\prime\in\mathcal{C}_d$, it may be impossible for them to differ at only one entry (see Example 1). With ${\mathrm rank} (\mathbf{D})=q$, $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^\prime\in\mathcal{C}_d$ may even differ for $q+1$ entries. This means individual’s contribution can no longer be looked into separately, but in groups as encoded in Definition 4. We believe this makes the study quite interesting as now the geometry “between” the entries in the datasets is accounted for, while differential privacy over metric spaces looks into geometry of individual entries in the datasets. 

We have added two new remarks, Remark 1, and Remark 2 on p3 of the rebuttal revision, to highlight these distinctions. 

Finally, we believe these clarifications have further made our contributions clear: 1) our work establishes differential privacy over affine manifolds with strong theoretical results (necessary and sufficient conditions, and protocols achieving tight privacy level); 2) the affine manifold captures the geometry between entries in databases as a nontrivial extension to differential privacy framework over metric spaces; 3) we found applications in cloud-based control systems where the proposed framework can be put in direct use. 

We would be grateful if you can re-evaluate the score on our paper. Privacy has become increasingly important for the area of machine learning and our work can be a useful reference for the conference. But regardless of that, we thank the continuous inputs which greatly help us understand the problem and write a clearer paper.

content.title: The neighbourhood definition is not applicable to the case with added or removed record as implied by the affine-manifold constraint
content.comment:
Thanks again for the prompt feedback. 

This work in fact focuses on the neighboring data by modifiying records  as implied by the affine manifold $\mathcal{C}_d\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, while for the neighbourhood by adding or removing record, the current neighbourhood definition is not applicable. To be precise, for any two $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^\prime$ in the affine manifold $\mathcal{C}_d$, they have already been assumed to have the same number of entries (i.e., $n$), which implies that $\mathbf{x}^\prime$ can be only obtained by modifying, instead of adding or removing, records in $\mathbf{x}$. Given the mentioned example $A\mathbf{x}=0$, if we add or remove $x_i$ in $\mathbf{x}$ to obtain $\mathbf{x}^\prime$, then we are unable to preserve the manifold $A\mathbf{x}^\prime=0$ as the dimensions between matrix $A$ and vector $\mathbf{x}^\prime$ are not compatible.

content.title: I see
content.comment:
Sorry for being imprecise, what I meant was having $A x_i = 0$ for any record, where $A \in R^{n \times k}$ and $x_i \in R^k$. That's a manifold, surely, and A does not have depend on the size of the dataset.

Similarly, defining the manifold to be the surface of a sphere or something, should have nothing to do with the dataset size.

content.title: Further response
content.comment:
Thanks very much for your prompt feedback and the patient explanation, and we now understand your concerns. 

If there is a set of manifolds $A_ix_i=0$ with $x_i\in\mathbb{R}^k$, we then can take the whole vector $x_i$ as a record and define a neighbourhood by adding or removing record $x_i$ surely without dimension compatible issue in the manifolds. Despite of this, we note that there comes the dimension compatible issue in the mechanism. Specifically, this work considers a linear mechanism of the form $M(\mathbf{x}) = F\mathbf{x}+\gamma$ with vector $\mathbf{x}$ being a collection of all $x_i$. Given the $\mathbf{x}^\prime$ after adding or removing a record, the dimensions between matrix $F$ and $\mathbf{x}^\prime$ turn out incompatible. In other words, given the linear mechanism $M(\mathbf{x}) = F\mathbf{x}+\gamma$ over the affine manifold, the neighbourhood definition by adding or removing record is not applicable.

Moreover, in this paper we study the affine manifold $\mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}=0$, which may not be separated into several independent manifolds $\mathbf{D}_i\mathbf{x}_i+\mathbf{b}_i=0$, e.g., the example in Section 4. As a result, the neighbourhood definition by adding or removing record is not applicable due to the dimension compatible issue in the manifold, as we addressed in the last response.

In the rebuttal revision, we have added a new remark to discuss the above points. Thanks again for your patient explanations.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2731 by Reviewer DL38

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper develops mechanisms for achieving differential privacy, when data are correlated in an affine way. An application to cloud-based control and numerical experiments are also presented.
content.main_review:
The paper discusses mechanisms to achieve differential privacy of data satisfying affine constraints. The motivation is explained both with an example and an application to a control problem. It provides a new notion of adjacency for the affine-correlated data and uses this to create to mechanisms for achieving diff. privacy (once with gaussian and once with laplacian noise). Numerical experiments also show that structured noise injection behaves better than random noises. 

I am not very familiar with the literature on differential privacy, thus I cannot provide a confident evaluation of the relation with related work and technical strength. Below are a few questions and critisism:

i) The term manifold-dependency in the title and the main paper seems a bit bold to me, I started reviewing thinking that this work has to do with Riemannian geometry. Since this is not the case and the data constraints are just affine, I would suggest to change the terminology to something like "differential privacy under affine constraints".

ii) As far as I understand, Example 1(ii) provides some worse case differential privacy levels for when data are affine-correlated. Can you prove that these levels are tight, i.e. someone cannot further improve on them?

iii) I struggle to understand the intuition behind the third line of equation (5) in the definition of adjacency, could you please provide more details on how this is related with the technicalities in the proof of privacy of your derived mechanisms?

iv) How do you practically compute $\sigma$ in equations (9) and (19)?

v) Second par. of related work, third line, seminar $\rightarrow$ seminal
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper builds on existent work on differential privacy and takes a reasonable step further to investigate mechanisms for when the data are dependent in a simple way. The motivation is well explained and numerics seem to be in favour of the presented methods. Thus I recommend acceptance, although I am not really familiar with the relevant literature to provide a confident review.

display_title: Points well taken and changes made correspondingly; Additional points explained in response below

content.title: Points well taken and changes made correspondingly; Additional points explained in response below
content.comment:
Thank you very much for the helpful comments, to which our responses are respectively given as below.


i): It is a good idea to add the word 'affine' so as to be more accurate and less misleading to the Riemannian geometry. The word 'dependency' has been adopted so that the notion is consistent with the relevant literature on differential privacy with data dependency. In view of this, we have modified the title as 'Differential privacy with affine-manifold data dependency.' 


ii): The answer is yes, and the established privacy budgets in Example 1 are indeed tight. In fact, for a scalar mechanism $\hat M(x)=ax+\gamma$ with $\gamma$ being a Laplace distribution with zero mean and variance $\sigma_\gamma^2$, it is known that it preserves the $(\epsilon,0)$-differential privacy with a tight level $\epsilon=a\mu/\sigma_\gamma$. With this in mind, taking Example 1(ii) into consideration, for privacy of $x_1$, releasing the output of the mechanism $M(x_1,x_2)$ with affine-manifold correlation is equivalent to releasing $x_1$ twice as $M_1(x_1)=x_1+\gamma_1$ and $M_2(x_1)=(x_1-b)/k+\gamma_2$,  achieving $(\epsilon_1,0)$- and  $(\epsilon_2,0)$-differential privacy with tight levels $\epsilon_1=\mu/\sigma_\gamma$ and $\epsilon_2=\mu/(k\sigma_\gamma)$. 

According to the sequential composability property of the differential privacy, the mechanism $M(x_1,x_2)$ achieves the differential privacy of $x_1$ with a tight level $\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2=(1+\frac{1}{k})\frac{\mu}{\sigma_\gamma}$. Similarly, we can prove that the mechanism $M(x_1,x_2)$ achieves the $((1+k)\frac{\mu}{\sigma_\gamma},0)$-differential privacy of $x_2$ tightly. In summary, it can be concluded that the mechanism $M(x_1,x_2)$ achieves the differential privacy of $(x_1,x_2)$ with a tight level $$
\max\{\Big((1+\frac{1}{k})\frac{\mu}{\sigma_\gamma},(1+k)\frac{\mu}{\sigma_\gamma}\Big)\},
$$ i.e., the $(g\epsilon,0)$-differential privacy in the paper with $g=\max\{\big(1+\frac{1}{k},(1+k)\big)\}$ and $\epsilon=\frac{\mu}{\sigma_\gamma}$.

iii): The affine manifold can be rewritten into a new form indicated in the equation before Definition 4 in our rebuttal revision. 
In view of this new form, it can be seen that the third equation of Eq (5) guarantees that the $\mathbf{x}'$ is drawn from the affine manifold $\mathcal{C}_{d}$. In this way, our manifold adjacency notion can capture the manifold dependency nature of the sensitive data, forming the intuition of introducing the third equation of Eq (5). To facilitate the readability of the paper, we have added such an equation in the revised paper. Regarding the relation of the third equation to the proof, it enables us to express the difference of the adjacent pair $(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')$ as a function of the difference between $x_i$ and $x_i'$ as shown in (29). In the revised paper, we have added more details on how the three equations in (5) are used in the proof. 

iv): For practical computation of  $\sigma$ from  (9) and (19), we have added some discussions on the design of $\sigma$ from (9) before section 3.2. In fact, there are two approaches: one is to adopt the numerical design algorithm in the work of Balle \& Wang (2018) to search for a tight $\sigma$, while the second is to use an analytical but less tight lower bound as $$
    \sigma \geq  ({\mu\bar\Delta_{\mathcal{N}}})/\Big(\sqrt{\Phi^{-2}(\delta)+2\epsilon} + \Phi^{-1}(\delta)\Big).
$$ For the design of $\sigma$ from (19), both approaches are still applicable as (9) and (19) are the same.
    
v): We have corrected this error. Thanks again.

content.comment:
Thank you very much for the positive evaluation of the paper organization and problem setting. We also appreciate the suggestions of the two interesting and relevant papers. 

In the suggested paper 1, a matrix mechanism is designed to answer a workload of linear counting queries with correlated noises to improve the utility; in the suggested paper 2, a matrix-variate Gaussian mechanism is calibrated by adding a matrix-valued noise drawn from a matrix-variate Gaussian distribution. In view of this, both papers are closely related to our paper in the sense of employing the noise structure as a noise calibration tool. 

In the meantime,   our paper studies the vector-valued mechanism with affine-manifold dependency data, which is an extension of the setup from the two suggested papers.  We have cited the two papers in the revised manuscript.
